documents.abstract: This article examines sharenting practices among parents in relation to the recognition of the child's agency and the underlying relational mechanisms, interpreted through the lens of Educational Transactional Analysis (ETA). The empirical study employed a questionnaire-based survey of N = 420 parents of children aged 6-15 attending primary schools in Poznań, Poland. Statistical analyses (Welch's t test, Pearson's χ² test) revealed a digital privacy paradox: despite widespread endorsement of children's right to privacy, as many as 61.6% of parents of children aged 6–15 do not always ask their children for consent before publishing their image, or do not always respect their answers. This practice illustrates the discounting of the child's digital sovereignty from a paternalistic life position. Mothers were more likely than fathers to approach sharenting relationally, seeking digital strokes through the Child ego state. Higher self-assessed knowledge co-occurred with stronger concerns about artificial intelligence and with a propensity for corrective action (41.7% of parents had deleted previously posted photos of their child). The shift toward a position that recognizes the child as a subject occurs in response to adolescents' resistance or to parental self-reflection. The pedagogical implications point to the need for workshops on relational digital maturity and for promoting digital consent from the earliest years.

Background: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) requires a coordinated and effective response, with non-technical skills (NTS) playing an important role in patient safety. Deficiencies in these skills may contribute to preventable clinical errors. Objectives: To map the scientific evidence on the contribution of simulation to the development of NTS among healthcare teams in the context of CPR. Methods: This scoping review followed JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting recommendations. MEDLINE, CINAHL, Nursing & Allied Health Collection: Comprehensive and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched via EBSCOhost up to 7 July 2026. Eligibility followed Population, Concept and Context criteria; two reviewers independently selected and charted the evidence. Results: The 27 included sources yielded three themes: simulation as a strategy for skill development; NTS in CPR; and complementary educational interventions. Communication was the most frequently reported NTS, alongside leadership, teamwork, situational awareness, and decision-making. Reported improvements varied across sources and skills, and some diminished or were only partially retained over time. Debriefing was addressed in 21 sources (77.8%). Evidence on complementary technologies remained preliminary, with some tools lacking formal evaluation or validation. Conclusions: The findings provide a descriptive map of heterogeneous evidence and suggest that simulation may support NTS development, particularly with structured debriefing. They do not establish effectiveness or effects on clinical outcomes. Robust quantitative and longitudinal studies using validated measures are needed to confirm observed trends and assess retention, transfer to practice, team performance, patient safety, and clinical outcomes.

The study measurements of the human body are applied in various fields today, viz., ergonomics, kinanthropometry, medical purposes, fashion and merchandising, online retailing, and many more. As our lives have become fast-paced over time to get the clothing or accessory items made especially for an individual, the ready-to-wear industry expanded on the formula of standardising sizes and creating apparel in bulk. Although to consider that the human physique has a fixed set of sizes that progress and regress based on a mathematical formula is a faulty system in itself. In this chapter, the authors discuss the same and apprise the problems and the solutions in the field of advanced anthropometry.

Abstract: The workforce skill requirements across industries have been fundamentally redefined by the fast transition brought about by Industry 4.0 technologies, which include automation, big data analytics, artificial intelligence (AI), and cyber-physical systems. In order to address dynamic and technology-driven skill gaps, traditional role-based talent management approaches are becoming less and less effective. Continuous learning and ongoing education are emphasised as essential components in preparing employees to adapt to the shifting demands of the industry. This study looks at how upskilling and reskilling programs driven by AI may close skill gaps in the Industry 4.0 ecosystem to acquire the workforce ready for the future. Through the use of AI-enabled learning, ongoing competency development, and digital adaptability, the study creates a conceptual framework that connects skill-based talent management practices (an independent variable) with workforce agility and organisational success (dependent factors). In order to gather opinions from managers and workers in technology-intensive businesses, the study uses a quantitative research approach and standardised survey tools.AI integration in talent development procedures improves strategic workforce planning, decreases skill obsolescence, and promotes cultures of continuous learning.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from a tool for information retrieval to a partner in conversation, advice, and emotional support. This integrative review examines whether that shift is reshaping friendship and other social bonds. Drawing on relationship science, human–machine communication research, surveys, experiments, longitudinal panels, randomized trials, and meta-analyses published through September 2026, including emerging evidence from Arab societies, the review develops the Responsiveness–Reciprocity Bridge Model to explain why conversational AI can relieve loneliness in the moment yet fail to build the relational capital that sustains people over time. A substantial minority of adolescents and young adults already turn to chatbots when they feel sad, anxious, or lonely, and short-term interactions with companion systems can reduce loneliness about as much as talking with another person, largely because users feel heard. These gains do not establish that synthetic ties can replace human friendship. Close relationships require mutual need, sacrifice, shared history, and practical solidarity that chatbots do not provide; in a randomized experiment, a human peer outperformed a highly supportive chatbot, and longitudinal and large-sample studies associate intensive, companionship-oriented use with greater loneliness and lower well-being. In Arab contexts, culturally aligned and human-guided digital tools show promise, but claims that AI is widely replacing traditional friends are not supported by comparable prevalence research. The central implication is balance: AI can widen access to support, but only if it is designed, governed, and used as a bridge to human relationships rather than as a substitute for them.

Purpose: This study aims to evaluate suitable foundation systems for a three-story building constructed on soft soil in the centre of Basra City, Iraq. The study assesses the structural response, bearing capacity, punching shear, and settlement behaviour of different foundation types to identify an appropriate and practical foundation solution. Design/Methodology/Approach: The structural analysis of the three-story building was performed using STAAD.Pro to determine the reactions at the building supports. Subsequently, SAFE was used to model and analyse different foundation systems, including isolated footings, strip footings, and mat foundations with and without beams. The foundation systems were evaluated based on punching shear and settlement criteria. Research Limitation: The study focuses on a three-story building and the specific soft-soil conditions of central Basra; therefore, the findings may not be directly applicable to buildings with significantly different heights or soil conditions. Findings: The results indicated that all investigated foundation systems satisfied the punching shear requirements. However, most isolated footings exceeded the permissible settlement limit of 25.4 mm. Although the strip footing remained within the allowable settlement limit, its application was considered impractical because of its limited economic feasibility and construction difficulties. The mat foundation modelled as a flat slab achieved a maximum settlement of 14 mm, while the mat foundation with beams recorded a maximum settlement of 19.8 mm. Practical Implication: The results indicate that mat foundations are suitable for low-rise buildings on soft soil. The mat foundation with beams provides a more economical alternative to the flat-slab mat foundation. Social Implication: Selecting an appropriate foundation system can improve building safety, reduce construction risks, and contribute to more reliable and sustainable urban development in areas characterised by soft soil. Originality/Value: This study compares foundation alternatives for low-rise buildings on soft soil in Basra, offering practical guidance for selecting safe and economically feasible foundation systems.

Generative AI has outpaced pedagogical and ethical guidance in accounting classrooms, leaving students and educators uncertain whether it supports or undermines the discipline's dual emphasis on procedural accuracy and professional judgment. To address this problem, this study examines how 92 business undergraduates perceive generative AI tools, notably ChatGPT, in accounting education, drawing on in-class, handwritten survey responses. Findings show that students view AI as a useful yet uncertain resource: valuing its speed, accessibility, and support while raising concerns over cheating, fairness, unclear institutional policies, and overreliance. Four interconnected themes emerged: Practical Affordances and Engagement, Ethical Tensions and Integrity, Curricular and Institutional Context, and Reflective Learning and Active Engagement. These results suggest student perceptions are shaped less by technology alone than by the pedagogical and ethical conditions of its introduction. Theoretically, the study identifies an augmentation–formation paradox specific to disciplines that combine codifiable procedure with professional judgment, which is advanced tentatively as extending the boundary conditions of paradox theory in education, a proposition that requires further empirical testing. Thematic analysis using a hybrid inductive–deductive coding strategy served as the primary analytic approach, supported by supplementary lexical analyses. The study contributes to management and accounting education by demonstrating that responsible AI integration requires clear guidance, reflective learning, and explicit alignment among AI use, assessment design, and academic integrity.

This paper starts from existing open-source weights, stacks new inference research on top of the optimization techniques already in use, and produces faster inference of the same model—without changing a single weight. Sushila.cpp is a free, local inference engine built on top of llama.cpp, the open-source engine behind Ollama, with SGLang on NVIDIA servers. Large language models are slow and expensive to run mainly because every generated token reads the model’s weights (for mixture-of-experts models, its active experts) from memory again. SUSHILA (Scalable Upstream Synthesis for Hybrid Inference in Large-model Acceleration) tests the published speed-up methods on each model once, right after its release, keeps those that make it faster at unchanged quality, and adds methods of our own. One of them, a landscape precomputed once per model, previews every next-token score cheaply, then computes only the best candidates exactly, reading 13–15% of the output layer with ≥99.75% agreement on the top token (7–70B models). Over eight GPU chat and coding models, Sushila.cpp achieves a geometric-mean speedup of 2.35× over Ollama (up to 4.05× on Llama-3.3-70B, on 160 benchmark prompts it never saw, with GSM8K accuracy unchanged within its error bars), measured on an NVIDIA A100 with Sushila.cpp’s SGLang serving path. Most of this gain comes from existing methods; our precomputed draft heads add 1–11% where a good head was already published and are most of the gain where none was: 3.64× on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B and 3.56× on Kimi-Dev-72B. Speed tests were done on one NVIDIA A100 80GB for chat and coding models (media mostly on one RTX 4090; engine-level tests also on CPUs), one user at a time; results may vary on other computers. Every result has its scripts and raw outputs in our public repository, and each chat and coding comparison reruns with one command.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has established a new technological and organizational landscape across all industries, yet the process of creating AI architecture remains disjointed, intuitive, and domain-oriented. The proposed study introduces a System-Analytical Framework of Artificial Intelligence Architecture Design (SA-AI Framework), a collection of principles from systems analysis and multi-criteria decision-making intended to harmonize architectural design processes across heterogeneous AI domains. The paper is based on twenty-five current studies in explainable AI, neural-symbolic architectures, human-centered robotics, agentic systems, and domain-specific applications, such as healthcare, finance, energy, and education, that inform a comparative synthesis of architectural design principles. A Research Design Science Research (DSR) approach is used to model and test the SA-AI Framework conceptually across four stages: requirements analysis, identification of architectural alternatives, multi-criteria evaluation, and model validation. Results show that the framework offers a systematic, defensible method for constructing AI architectures, enabling greater exposure, flexibility, and decision-making effectiveness. It has cohesively unified the different models of AI, including the agentic AI, Explainable AI (XAI), Human-Centered AI (HCAI), and safety-driven architectures, providing both theory and practice to AI engineering and policy design. This paper concludes that system analysis helps design AI systems that integrate both technical and socio-technical systems to enhance the governance, reliability, and sustainability of intelligent architecture in the next generation.

To read the full-text Open Access article and download the PDFs, please visit our Issue portal at Paradigm (Walter de Gruyter): https://reference-global.com/article/10.56508/mhgcj.v9i1.374 Introduction: Workplace mental health promotion in higher education requires attention to how digital technologies reshape teaching demands and resources. Purpose: To identify perceived demands and resources surrounding teacher-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) and interpret their implications for teachers’ mental health promotion. Methodology: An exploratory mixed-methods study combined a survey of 150 participants (56 English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers and 94 students/student-tutors) with 12 teacher interviews at two Ukrainian universities in January-February 2026. Descriptive statistics and four exploratory Fisher exact tests with Holm adjustment were integrated with thematic analysis of 30 selected translated interview extracts. Job Demands-Resources and self-determination theories informed a post-hoc interpretation. Results: Among teachers, 53.6% rated an AI platform for EFL teachers (Twee) very useful for preparation-time saving and 57.1% for task variety. Across the mixed sample, access (27.3%), quality assurance (22.0%), curriculum alignment (20.0%), and training/time (20.0%) were the leading constraints. Interview extracts linked anticipated workload relief to individual student support, while highlighting learning demands and the importance of professional judgment, empathy, and mentoring. Conclusions: These perceptions identify work-design issues relevant to mental health promotion during AI implementation. Participatory decisions, protected learning and recovery time, and accessible psychosocial support are priorities for institutional consideration

This thesis analyzes teachers’ pedagogical decision-making in selecting and adapting artificial intelligence-generated academic texts for Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT) in the context of teaching English as a foreign language (EFL) in Uzbekistan. The study considers texts generated by generative AI tools not as ready-to-use teaching materials, but as resources that require linguistic, content-related, and methodological evaluation and adaptation by teachers to suit specific learning tasks. Particular attention is paid to teachers’ decisions based on lexical and grammatical complexity, content accuracy and reliability, students’ language proficiency, the characteristics of academic discourse, the communicative purpose of the task, and relevance to the local educational context. The study also systematizes adaptation strategies such as simplifying and shortening texts, replacing lexical items, contextualizing content, and transforming texts into TBLT tasks. The analysis demonstrates that artificial intelligence does not automatically guarantee pedagogically appropriate materials and that the quality of the final learning materials depends on teachers’ professional judgment, linguistic competence, and methodological decisions.

Intensive English Programs have undergone major changes in how technology supports language education and research. At the University of Pittsburgh&s;s English Language Institute, early efforts centered on custom-built software that supported both classroom instruction and research, culminating in projects such as the PELIC corpus. Over time, however, there has been an industry-wide shift toward off-the-shelf platforms emphasizing usability and integration, often at the cost of research adaptability. Throughout these shifts, work in linguistics, applied linguistics, and related fields (such as second language studies, corpus linguistics, and psycholinguistics) have remained a key influence, and these areas have been strongly influenced by the scholarship of Alan Juffs. Looking ahead, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as large language models offer personalized learning opportunities but also pose risks. They challenge assumptions about the assessment of linguistic proficiency and complicate future research by undermining the provenance of learner-provided text. The PELIC corpus, completed under Juffs’ leadership just before the rise of GenAI, serves as a gift to future research, capturing robust learner data from the “pre-AI” era.

This study examines how pedagogical innovation can support Generation Z students in post-COVID marketing education, where hybrid learning and artificial intelligence are reshaping course design. It introduces the Pedagogical Innovation Pentagon, an evidence-informed model organized around five interrelated dimensions: hybridization, digitalization, artificial intelligence, responsibility, and harmonization. The model was developed and evaluated through a mixed-methods exploratory study conducted with first-year students enrolled in a bilingual introductory marketing course within a multi-campus business program. The model was implemented through an Instructional Capsule, a structured learning environment combining bilingual content development, guided activities, feedback mechanisms, sustainability-focused case studies, and shared assessment practices across campuses. Student self-reports and course analytics were used to explore how this instructional approach supported engagement, clarity, feedback, ethical awareness, and coherence in students’ learning experiences. Findings suggest that effective innovation in marketing education depends less on technological sophistication than on the meaningful integration of digital tools within a human-centered and ethically intentional learning environment. The study contributes to marketing education by offering a transferable approach for integrating digital transformation, AI, and responsible pedagogy into course design and continuous improvement.

Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to personalize science instruction, yet evidence regarding teachers’ AI-supported practices and learners’ cognitive engagement remains limited. This study examined Grade 8 Science teachers’ practices embedded with AI-driven adaptive learning systems at Bongabon National High School, Nueva Ecija, during school year 2026–2027. Specifically, it described teachers’ profiles and practices across planning and preparation, classroom environment, instruction, and professional responsibilities, and investigated relationships and differences in respondents’ perceptions. A descriptive survey design with quasi-experimental designation, involved six Grade 8 Science teachers and 499 students. Teacher respondents were covered through complete enumeration, while student respondents were selected through simple random sampling. Questionnaires provided data analyzed using frequencies, percentages, weighted means, t-tests, and Spearman’s rho. Findings indicated that AI-embedded teaching practices were “Always Practiced,” with an overall grand weighted mean of 3.60. Classroom environment obtained the highest combined domain mean (3.64), followed by instruction (3.62), planning and preparation (3.59), and professional responsibilities (3.55). Teachers’ educational attainment showed significant negative relationships with planning and preparation (rho = −0.892) and classroom environment (rho = −0.874), whereas other profile variables showed no significant relationships. Teachers’ and learners’ perceptions did not differ significantly across domains. The study concluded that AI-supported teaching practices were consistently reported and recommended targeted professional development and activities to strengthen comparatively less-practiced areas. These findings may guide context-responsive integration of adaptive learning tools in junior high school Science instruction while supporting reflective teaching practice and student engagement. This supports responsible implementation.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has introduced new paradigms for teaching, learning, and assessment, especially in the development of students’ writing performance. This meta-analysis examines the effectiveness of blended, technology-enhanced, and AI-supported instructional interventions on student learning outcomes. Eleven studies representing 477 participants across primary, secondary, and higher-education settings were synthesized. The included studies represented heterogeneous educational contexts and assessed outcomes such as academic achievement, literacy, vocabulary and language learning, digital literacy, and motivation. Accordingly, the pooled effect represents an overall effect on student learning outcomes rather than a writing-proficiency-specific effect. Studies were identified through ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar and represented 477 participants across elementary, secondary, and higher-education settings and diverse disciplinary contexts. The results revealed a large and statistically significant pooled effect size [Hedges’ g = 0.89, 95% CI (0.76, 1.10)], showing that students who participated in technology-enhanced instructional interventions outperformed those receiving traditional instruction. Exploratory moderator analyses showed differences according to educational level, intervention duration, and technology type, with primary and secondary students, medium-length interventions (4–8 weeks), and interactive tools showing the strongest effects. The findings show the potential of thoughtfully integrated digital and AI-supported tools to enhance teaching and learning.

This study investigates the psychological mechanisms through which artificial intelligence (AI) literacy relates to L2 learners’ willingness to write (WTW). It proposes a serial mediation model wherein L2 writing self-efficacy (WSE) and L2 writing anxiety (WA) sequentially mediate this relationship. Grounded in social cognitive theory and control-value theory, the research employed a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design with 303 Chinese EFL learners. Quantitative results from structural equation modeling indicate that: (1) L2 WSE fully mediates the relationship between AI literacy and L2 WTW; (2) AI literacy is indirectly linked to L2 WTW through a sequential pathway: by first positively predicting L2 WSE, which in turn negatively predicts L2 WA; and (3) the direct effects of AI literacy on L2 WA and L2 WTW are non-significant. To explain these quantitative pathways, qualitative interviews with 16 participants further elucidated how AI tool usage corresponds to higher L2 WSE through strategic partnership, reduced startup burden, and task scaffolding support. Furthermore, the qualitative narratives revealed that while AI usage can initially be associated with anxiety (e.g., fear of exposure, tool-related frustration), the heightened L2 WSE linked to AI literacy effectively serves as a protective factor against these affective barriers. The study concludes that AI literacy positively correlates with L2 WTW through a fully indirect mechanism, in which heightened L2 WSE serves as a vital prerequisite for lowering L2 WA. These findings contribute to theory by integrating two major psychological frameworks and offer practical implications for leveraging AI to cultivate more willing L2 writers.

Digitalization is transforming the workplace and the way of doing business in various sectors.Industry 4.0, commonly known as the fourth industrial revolution, has changed the way people work, develop, manage, control, hire and interact with each other.Indeed, we are witnessing a change in the nature of jobs.Today, muscle jobs are disappearing and brain jobs are growing, and labor-based industries are coming from skill-based industries and will have to be replaced by knowledge-based industries.In this extremely aggressive situation where everyone interacts with each other, technology and innovation are transforming the world into a global village worldwide.Artificial intelligence helps companies perform any function more effectively and efficiently.The purpose of this research is to conduct a bibliometric analysis of the scientific literature that addresses the application and impact of artificial intelligence in the field of human resource management in a connected way.At the same time the topic is quite new and this paper will contribute to scientific researches in the form of theoretical background.In the article literature review related to the topic will be used.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: In 2016, a leading AI researcher predicted that machine learning would render radiologists obsolete within five years. A decade later, the opposite has happened. Radiology is among the most competitive specialties in medicine, and artificial intelligence has become a tool that makes physicians faster, more accurate, and more capable rather than a force that replaces them. This chapter traces that shift across radiology, pathology, ophthalmology, cardiology, and stroke and diabetic eye care, where AI now detects disease, triages urgent cases, and extends screening to populations that were previously underserved. The recurring lesson is that augmentation, not automation, defines AI’s clinical value, and that its safe and effective use depends on physicians who understand both its capabilities and its limits. By establishing this framing, the chapter sets up the practical questions the rest of the book addresses: how to evaluate AI tools, integrate them into clinical workflows, navigate the ethical challenges they raise, and redefine physician expertise for a new era of medicine.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The dominance of Euro-American frameworks in industrial and organizational psychology has rendered culturally embedded work experiences largely invisible. While foundational models such as the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework elegantly illuminate universal engagement mechanisms across diverse contexts, occupational health literature has traditionally paid less attention to how intersecting racialized and gendered identities shape occupational well-being in postcolonial settings. This conceptual paper addresses this contextual gap by examining the organizational position of Black women in South African middle management, a group navigating unique structural tensions rooted in historical exclusion and contemporary marginalization. Responding to calls for disciplinary decolonization, I propose an integrated Afrocentric framework that brings Bosadi theorization into conversation with salutogenic principles. Specifically, I argue that Bosadi identity functions are not merely as a demographic marker but as a culturally embedded personal resource that shapes how job demands are interpreted, managed, and made meaningful. By positioning identity as an analytic resource rather than a contextual variable, the framework extends the JD-R model’s explanatory power to account for culturally specific modes of resilience and meaning-making. The paper concludes by outlining theoretical contributions to organizational psychology and offering directions for empirical research, including methodological considerations for studying culturally situated work experiences. This work aims to support the development of organizational practices that are genuinely responsive to the lived realities of historically marginalized women.

This study aimed to synthesize, develop, and evaluate the Micro Game-Based Learning Model on Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment. The study integrated Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and Metaverse technologies to create a learning environment that provides short learning units, interactive game-based activities, and simulated communication situations. The research objectives were to (1) synthesize the learning process, (2) develop the learning model, and (3) evaluate the learning model. The evaluation panel consisted of three experts from various academic institutions. The experts were selected based on their experience at least 3 years in education, instructional design and development, particularly in teaching English for communication. The research instruments consisted of the learning model, learning platform, and an expert evaluation questionnaire based on a 5-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics according to the research objectives. The findings indicated that the appropriateness of the developed learning model was evaluated at a highest level (Mean = 4.93, SD = 0.24). The findings suggest that integrating Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and an Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment provides a feasible approach for developing technology-supported English communication learning.

The pressure to implement formative evaluation of English in colleges and universities is increasing day by day, and the massive and complex learning data increases the burden of teachers' evaluation. Artificial intelligence can run through the whole evaluation process, improve evaluation efficiency, and promote the transformation of digital teaching for teachers. This paper takes college English teachers as the object, relies on multi-source data to build an analysis framework, and explores the relationship between AI-empowered formative evaluation and teachers' digital competence. The research shows that teachers' AI application has the characteristics of staged evolution, digital ability differentiates with the degree of AI integration, and the overall competency improvement effect is obviously stratified. This study improves the relevant theoretical system, and also provides practical reference for teacher training, intelligent teaching platform optimization and evaluation reform. AI has become a key boost to reshape the evaluation model and enhance teachers' digital literacy.

This chapter examines how circular economy (CE) imaginaries are articulated and stabilised within the fashion industry. Drawing on the concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, it analyses the Global Fashion Summit 2025 as a field-configuring event where competing visions of circular transition are publicly performed. Based on participant observation, session recordings, and field notes, the study identifies five distinct CE imaginaries. The findings show that these imaginaries stabilise unevenly through discourses, representations, institutions, and identities, shaping how circularity becomes actionable. The chapter contributes to fashion business and management research by demonstrating that CE transition is not governed by a single coherent pathway, but constructed through multiple co-existing visions that prioritise different problems, solutions, and actors.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming foreign language learning from traditional knowledge transmission into a data-driven adaptive learning process. Grounded in Personalized Learning Theory and technology-enhanced learning (TEL), this study examines the impact of AI application on Korean language learning performance (KAP) from the perspective of technological mediation and further explores the mediating role of intelligent recommendation systems (IRSs). Using questionnaire and academic performance data from 850 undergraduate students majoring in the Korean language, the study employs multiple regression and mediation analysis to test the proposed relationships. The results indicate that AI application significantly improves KAP (β = 4.684, p < 0.01) and exerts a significant partial mediating effect through IRSs. Specifically, AI application significantly increases the utilization of IRSs (β = 3.127, p < 0.01), while IRSs further enhance learning performance (β = 2.827, p < 0.01). Marginal effect analysis further reveals that the positive effect of AI is strongest at moderate usage levels, whereas excessive AI use leads to diminishing marginal returns. The findings demonstrate that AI not only directly improves learning outcomes through real-time feedback, speech recognition, and personalized learning support, but also promotes resource allocation optimization and dynamic learning path adjustment through AI-driven adaptive learning mechanisms. This study extends the mechanism-oriented explanation of AI-assisted language learning within the context of Korean language education and provides theoretical and practical implications for the development of intelligent and personalized Korean language learning platforms in higher education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Abstract. The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for improving English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, particularly in the development of speaking proficiency. AI-powered chatbots, speech recognition systems, conversational agents, and generative AI applications enable learners to practise English, receive immediate feedback, and engage in interactive communication beyond the traditional classroom. This article examines the potential impact of AI-assisted learning on EFL learners’ speaking proficiency, with particular attention to the educational context of Uzbek universities. It explores the ways in which AI-based tools may support speaking fluency, pronunciation, grammatical accuracy, vocabulary development, learner confidence, and willingness to communicate. Drawing on existing research and pedagogical perspectives, the article discusses the opportunities and limitations of integrating AI into higher education. Particular attention is given to speaking anxiety, unequal access to digital resources, feedback reliability, learner autonomy, and the importance of teacher guidance. The analysis suggests that AI can serve as a valuable supplementary resource when integrated into structured pedagogical activities. However, its effectiveness depends on learners’ engagement, instructional design, and the combination of technological practice with authentic human interaction. Further empirical research involving Uzbek university students is necessary to establish the extent and long-term effects of AI-assisted speaking instruction. Keywords: artificial intelligence, EFL learners, speaking proficiency, AI-assisted learning, university students, conversational AI, language anxiety, Uzbekistan, digital education.

The fast growth of surveillance technology has drastically changed India's balance amongst individual liberty and political authority.Inconceivable amounts of data collection and behaviors analysis have been made possible by the combination of electronic tracking systems, AI (artificial intelligence), and sophisticated analysis of data.Although the legal framework created following the Apex Court's landmark decision in Honorable K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India recognized privacy or as essential rights (Fundamental right) within Article 21, it is still mostly restricted to the instructive and corporeal dimensions of confidentiality 1 .This study explores the idea of the "monitoring of thinking," which refers to electronically facilitated methods that use data trends and electronic (digital) behavioral assessment to infer, anticipate, and possibly affect humans thinking.Intellectual observation works by creating mental profiling and prediction models that disclose opinions, choices, and desires, in contrast with conventional observation, which concentrates on tracking activities or telecommunications .2Substantial constitutional issues are raised by such activities, especially in relation to liberty of expressing itself, psychological independence, and decency.The danger is increased by the potential for cognitive regulation and computational tampering which could stifle independent thinking and participatory engagement.The article makes the case that supreme law (Constitutional law) has a "silent blind zone" because it does not identify and control incursions into the intellectual realm.Judicial and parliamentary advances have not specifically tackled intellectual freedom or mental confidentiality, notwithstanding Puttaswamy expansive concept of confidentiality.This study shows that current statutory safeguards are inadequate to adequately safeguard people from the growing risks of mental monitoring via conceptual study and involvement with modern technical circumstances.3 As reaction, the article argues that Art.21 of Constitution should recognize a fresh basic entitlement (Right) to mental confidentiality or intellectual autonomy.In order to prevent advances in technology from undermining the fundamental principles of liberty, integrity, and democratization, it closes by highlighting the necessity of focused parliamentary improvements, judiciary creativity, and strong organizational safeguarding.

Work stress is a common occupational health problem among teachers and may affect psychological well-being and the quality of teaching. One factor suspected to be associated with work stress is job satisfaction. This study aimed to analyze the relationship between job satisfaction and work stress among teachers at SMP Negeri 14 and SMP Negeri 18, South Tangerang City. This study employed a quantitative design with a cross-sectional approach. The study population consisted of 96 active teachers from both schools, with 93 teachers meeting the study criteria and participating through total sampling. Data were collected using a respondent characteristics questionnaire, the Job Satisfaction Survey (JSS) to measure job satisfaction, and the Job Stress Scale to measure work stress. Data analysis included univariate and bivariate analyses using the Chi-Square test at a 95% significance level. The results showed that 39.8% of respondents had low job satisfaction, 25.8% were categorized as ambivalent, and 34.4% had high job satisfaction. Most respondents (65.6%) experienced low work stress, while 34.4% experienced high work stress. Bivariate analysis revealed a significant relationship between job satisfaction and work stress (p < 0.001; OR = 8.27; 95% CI: 3.06–22.39), indicating that teachers with low job satisfaction had a higher risk of experiencing work stress than those with high job satisfaction. In addition, age, gender, and teaching workload were significantly associated with work stress. The study concludes that improving job satisfaction through improvements in the work environment, reward systems, organizational communication, and workload management is an important strategy for reducing work stress and enhancing teachers’ well-being.

This paper critically examines the persistent responsibility gap in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), arguing that current approaches fail to adequately bridge it. While XAI is often promoted as a remedy for the opacity of AI systems—the so-called “black box problem”—and as a way to enable human accountability in both high- and low-stakes AI applications, I contend that these hopes are premature. The paper distinguishes between legal and moral responsibility, arguing that regulation alone cannot address the full spectrum of responsibility gaps, especially in everyday, low-stakes scenarios. Then, I argue that XAI needs to tackle two separate but interconnected problems in its attempt to bridge the responsibility gap: an epistemological problem concerning the nature of XAI explanations, and a moral attribution problem regarding the distribution of blame and praise in situations where AI is involved in decision-making. Through detailed discussion of XAI methods and their limitations, I demonstrate that existing techniques often provide only post-hoc, technically focused explanations, which are insufficient for grounding moral responsibility. The paper concludes that without fundamental advances in both the design of explanations and our practices of responsibility attribution, the responsibility gap in AI will remain an unresolved and pressing issue for the field.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in learning management systems (LMS) in higher education. It analyses how AI can support personalized learning, automated assessment, intelligent tutoring, learning analytics, and teachers’ instructional work. A conceptual approach is used to synthesize relevant literature and identify practical integration principles. The analysis indicates that AI-enabled LMS functions may improve the timeliness of feedback, help identify learning difficulties, and support evidence-informed educational decisions. However, these benefits are not automatic: they depend on pedagogical design, data quality, transparency, privacy safeguards, and meaningful human oversight. The article proposes a functional integration model that connects learner data, AI-based analysis, personalized recommendations, an intelligent assistant, and teacher review. Since the study is conceptual, the proposed model requires empirical evaluation before claims about its effectiveness can be made.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The awareness and perspectives of Scandinavian optometrists regarding artificial intelligence (AI) in eye care was evaluated through a web-based questionnaire. Responses from 421 optometrists were analyzed for familiarity, perceived benefits, concerns, and willingness to engage with AI technologies. Most participants expressed familiarity with AI and support for its inclusion in education and practice, though concerns regarding diagnostic accuracy and potential impacts on the patient-optometrist relationship were noted. These findings are critical for informing educational strategies and facilitating knowledge exchange aimed at addressing uncertainties and optimising the benefits of AI in eye care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This paper examines the multifaceted contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) to urban flood-risk reduction, with particular emphasis on data-driven forecasting, real-time monitoring, infrastructure management, emergency response, recovery, and resilient urban planning. AI technologies—including machine learning, predictive analytics, remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) networks, natural language processing, and image analysis—can support more accurate flood prediction, dynamic risk assessment, optimized drainage operations, and timely public communication. The paper also discusses the integration of AI into smart-city frameworks, the limitations of conventional flood-management approaches, challenges associated with data quality and availability, computational requirements, ethical considerations, and the need for interdisciplinary collaboration. In addition, an embedding-based long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture is presented for probabilistic streamflow forecasting in settings in which individual weather products may be unavailable. However, effective implementation requires robust data infrastructures, transparent model-development practices, appropriate institutional capacity, and supportive policy frameworks.

Abstract Motivation is central to successful English language learning because it influences effort, persistence, participation, and willingness to communicate. This thesis examines how gamification can support student motivation through a literature-based analysis of recent research. It argues that selected game elements may increase engagement when they promote competence, autonomy, meaningful progress, and social interaction. However, gamification is not automatically effective. Its value depends on careful alignment with language objectives, learner needs, and balanced classroom implementation. Keywords: EFL learners, engagement, gamification, intrinsic motivation, language learning, student motivation, willingness to communicate

This dissertation investigates the displacement of human actors by generative AI performers in the fastest-growing segment of the screen entertainment economy: the vertical drama, or micro-drama, industry. The study is organized around a triggering case widely reported in October 2026, in which a nineteen-year-old actress, Hannah Lowery, was reportedly recast out of an ice-skating-themed series when the production shifted entirely to AI-generated performers. Using the video report as an entry point, the dissertation triangulates its claims against primary trade reporting, including Business Insider (June 2026), trade publications such as Variety, Mashable, and The Economic Times, regulatory documents, and a broad interdisciplinary literature spanning cultural economics, labor sociology, media theory, and machine learning. Methodologically, the dissertation combines (i) documentary and content analysis of the video case and its verification status, examining each claim individually; (ii) economic analysis of production cost structures, drawing on reported estimates of US$1,000–US$3,000 per AI-generated episode compared with US$100,000–US$300,000 for equivalent productions featuring human casts; (iii) institutional analysis of the emerging regulatory landscape, including the 2023 SAG-AFTRA agreements, California Assembly Bill 2602 (AB 2602), Tennessee’s ELVIS Act, the proposed federal NO FAKES Act, the European Union’s AI Act, and China’s provisions governing deep synthesis and generative AI; and (iv) the construction of forward-looking scenarios for the coming decade. The central argument is threefold. First, vertical dramas constitute a genuine entry-level market for synthetic performance in a manner consistent with disruption theory: their economics are driven by cost minimization and production volume rather than the premium emotional differentiation characteristic of high-end productions. Second, the displacement pressure documented in 2026 is driven less by audience preferences than by production-cost arbitrage and platformization dynamics. Survey evidence indicates that Western audiences still overwhelmingly prefer human stars, whereas Chinese production has already shifted substantially toward AI-generated content. Third, the emerging legal and ethical framework—encompassing consent, compensation, disclosure, and posthumous rights—will determine whether the industry converges toward regulated coexistence or experiences a cascade of substitutions with severe consequences for the talent pipeline. The dissertation contributes a verified factual foundation, a production cost-structure model, a four-scenario matrix, and a policy agenda for performers, producers, platforms, and regulators. Approximate main-text word count: 31,000.Figures: 7.Tables: 9.

This study aims to describe the use of English songs as learning media and to analyze their role in increasing students’ motivation to learn English at SMP Alfaqih Muqaddam Kubu Raya. A descriptive qualitative approach was employed, involving 20 eighth-grade students and one English teacher as an informant. The songs used in the learning activities were Let It Go and Heal the World. Data were collected through classroom observations, semi-structured interviews, questionnaires, and documentation, and were analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings indicate that the use of English songs created a more engaging learning environment and encouraged students’ active participation. Observation results showed that 90% of the students were willing to repeat and practice the lyrics, 85% demonstrated enthusiasm during the learning process, and 80% paid attention while listening to the songs. Questionnaire results also revealed a high level of motivation, with an average score of 4.25 for the statement regarding increased motivation to learn English through songs. In addition to enhancing motivation, songs helped students retain vocabulary, improve pronunciation, build confidence, and experience a more enjoyable learning atmosphere. Let It Go particularly encouraged students’ confidence and courage, while Heal the World provided meaningful messages that supported intrinsic motivation. Despite several challenges, including difficulty understanding certain lyrics, pronunciation problems, and shyness when singing, these difficulties could be minimized through teacher guidance and repeated practice. Therefore, English songs can serve as practical, engaging, and effective learning media for supporting students’ motivation in learning English.

Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

The development of artificial intelligence is predominantly assessed in terms of increasing cognitive performance. Yet this comparison presupposes a yardstick that captures the diversity of possible forms of intelligence only incompletely. The Theory of Attractor Horizons advances the thesis that intelligent systems, by virtue of their respective organization, can reach different regions of cognitive attractors that may partly overlap without being wholly contained within one another. Greater performance within one organizational form does not confer general access to the organizational possibilities of other forms. The theory explains this asymmetry through the dependence of reachable attractors on available transformation pathways and examines aggregation as a mechanism that can give rise to new organizational forms while also restricting existing possibilities. From this follows the far-reaching prediction that artificial systems will develop structures of thought whose internal organization the human brain cannot itself instantiate within its biological form of intelligence, even where individual results remain verifiable or technically useful. Conversely, human organizational attractors may exist that remain inaccessible to artificial systems despite their superior cognitive performance. For alignment, this entails limits to understanding-based oversight and requirements for verifiable coexistence between different forms of intelligence.

Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Islamic education requires a pedagogical model that preserves teachers’ epistemic authority while addressing adolescents’ health needs. This study examines the implementation, pedagogical affordances, and limitations of ChatGPT-assisted Fiqh al-Ṭahārah learning and develops a model for strengthening Islamic value-based reproductive health literacy. Employing a qualitative single-case study design, the research was conducted at MA Al Ishlah Banjarejo Blora. Data were collected through observations, semi-structured interviews, documentation, and analysis of students’ interactions with ChatGPT, and were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña. The findings revealed three stages of implementation: preparation, inquiry-based interaction, and reflection and verification. ChatGPT provided a psychologically safer space for sensitive questions, flexible access to explanations, contextualized Fiqh learning, increased engagement, and critical AI literacy. However, its use was constrained by potential inaccuracies, oversimplification of differences among Islamic legal schools, prompt quality, unequal access, and privacy and ethical concerns. The resulting AI-Assisted Thaharah Learning Model integrates AI-assisted inquiry, teacher facilitation, source verification, and Islamic value internalization while maintaining teachers’ pedagogical, epistemic, and moral authority.

Human–computer interaction (HCI) has traditionally relied on assumptions of a relatively uniform user. Neurodiversity challenges this premise by highlighting variation in perception, attention, communication, and sensory processing. Advances in multimodal sensing, artificial intelligence (AI), and adaptive interfaces increasingly enable systems to respond to changing user needs in real time. This paper proposes an evidence-informed taxonomy for empathic adaptive interaction design, developed through a structured interdisciplinary review and conceptual synthesis. The taxonomy comprises six dimensions: User Cognitive Profile, Empathic Inference Capability, Sensing Modality, Adaptation Strategy, Application Context, and Governance, Autonomy, and Ethics. Together, these dimensions provide a structured framework for analyzing how systems sense user state, infer support needs, adapt interaction, and maintain transparency and user control. The framework supports the systematic analysis, comparison, design, evaluation, and future empirical validation of inclusive, neuroadaptive, and multimodal interaction systems responsive to cognitive diversity.

Abstract Generative AI is likely to transform terminology work by creating new opportunities for automation. At the same time, it raises concerns about the future of terminologists and terminological resources, as efficiency pressures may encourage excessive automation based on the perception that human expertise can be replaced by AI. However, large language models remain unreliable for terminological purposes due to errors, hallucinations, and various forms of bias, making terminologists indispensable for ensuring the accuracy and reliability of terminological data. This paper argues that human-centered AI, an approach that emphasizes that AI’s primary goal should be to contribute to human well-being, provides a framework for maximizing the benefits of generative AI while mitigating its risks. It contends that high levels of automation and meaningful human control are compatible and desirable, and that AI should enhance terminologists’ capabilities while preserving their agency and decision-making authority. The implications of AI-assisted terminology work are examined through three interrelated dimensions: the augmented terminologist, ethical AI, and human-centered design. In particular, the paper addresses how AI integration reshapes the role of the terminologist, affects professional values and working conditions, requires the management of AI-generated bias, and calls for the design of AI tools around the terminologist’s needs. The paper concludes that a human-centered orientation is necessary to ensure that AI strengthens, rather than undermines, the essential role of terminology work in supporting specialized communication and the accurate transmission of knowledge across languages and cultures.

documents.abstract: Clinical communication is a fundamental skill that impacts patient satisfaction, treatment adherence, and clinical outcomes. Traditional training methods, such as standardized patients (SPs) or virtual standardized patients (VSPs), face barriers including high costs, logistical complexity, and lack of spontaneous interaction. This study addresses these challenges by developing a scalable alternative based on Large Language Models (LLMs) to train medical students in the anamnesis phase. We developed an interactive Conversational Virtual Patient (CVP) system, understood here as a text- and voice-based simulated patient without graphical embodiment. The conversational logic is orchestrated as an explicit state machine over the interview, implemented with LangGraph, a graph-based framework in which each node performs one processing stage and a shared state persists across turns. Clinical consistency across the interview is maintained by a semantic memory layer implemented with LangMem, a library that stores clinical facts as vector embeddings and retrieves them by similarity. Performance is measured by an automatic evaluation module assessing 24 communication criteria derived from validated instruments such as the Communication Assessment Tool (CAT) and the Communication Skills Scale (CSS). The platform was validated with 21 participants, comprising 9 eighth-semester medical students, 11 practising physicians, and 1 expert in healthcare technology. All sessions were conducted in Spanish. Considering the student cohort, which addresses the educational utility of the tool, the system obtained a Chatbot Usability Questionnaire (CUQ) score of 82.3/100 and an average acceptance of the automated feedback of 4.50/5. The physician and expert cohort, which provides expert clinical validation, obtained 96.5/100 and 4.21/5 respectively, yielding a pooled usability score of 90.4/100 and a pooled feedback acceptance of 4.33/5. In an exploratory comparison against eleven physician ratings of the same interviews, rank agreement was highest for “Interest” ( $$\rho = 0.64$$ ) and lowest for “Completeness” ( $$\rho = 0.09$$ ), and the automated scores fell below the physician scores in every dimension. No dimension attained significance after correction for six comparisons, and the confidence intervals were wide, so these coefficients describe the observed sample rather than the agreement attainable in general. The results support the feasibility of the system as a complement to traditional medical training, providing immediate and standardized feedback. Given the sample size and the single-institution design, these findings should be read as an initial validation of feasibility and acceptability rather than as evidence of pedagogical efficacy.

documents.abstract: Purpose Grounded in the Social Information Processing Theory (SIPT), the current study aims to examine the role of Diversity-focused HR Practices in promoting Inclusion Climate; simultaneously, it also investigates the role of Inclusive Leadership as a moderator in relationship explaining how it shapes inclusion at work. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional quantitative approach has been taken, and the survey data were collected from 232 professionals employed in Indian IT sector organizations. To perform the data analysis PLS-SEM was employed using SmartPLS4.1.0 software. Findings The findings reveal while diversity-focused HR practices contribute to fostering an inclusive climate, their impact depends significantly on leadership behavior. Inclusive leaders play a critical role in strengthening the effectiveness of these practices by shaping how employees experience inclusion in their teams. Practical implications The findings of the study imply the gravity that a leader holds in the workgroup. As exhibited by findings, leaders with their inclusive behavior act as a catalyst which transforms HR practices into an inclusive workplace. Therefore, investments in diversity policies must be accompanied by leadership development programs to convert formal initiatives into employees-lived workplace experience. Originality/value The study integrates HR practices and leadership perspectives by identifying inclusive leadership as a contextual boundary condition explaining variability in inclusion climate formation. This shifts scholarly attention from formal HR systems to the role of leaders as enablers of inclusion, demonstrating that leadership is a key mechanism through which diversity initiatives translate into meaningful workplace experiences, thereby providing a novel insight to the present literature.

This study maps the importance, perceived needs, and competency gap of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) across four domains—Technical, Strategic, Ethical, Adaptive—and examines their associations with trust, adoption maturity, and industry context. Data were collected from 389 industry professionals in Indonesia using purposive and snowball sampling. The analysis employed descriptive statistics, Spearman correlation, Kruskal-Wallis H tests, and post-hoc Mann-Whitney U tests. The results indicate relatively high perceived GenAI competency needs across all domains, with the largest perceived gaps in the Technical and Strategic domains. Trust in GenAI was positively associated with perceived competency needs across all four domains and with perceived competency gaps in the Technical, Strategic, and Adaptive domains, but not the Ethical domain. Adoption maturity was associated with differences in several dimensions of industry perceptions, particularly industry-perceived graduate readiness to adopt GenAI and perceived needs in the Adaptive and Strategic domains. Sectoral differences were limited, with significant variation observed only in industry-perceived graduate readiness. The study contributes an integrated perspective linking trust and adoption maturity with perceived GenAI competency needs and gaps in Indonesia, highlighting curricular areas that warrant greater attention to applied Technical and Strategic capabilities across organizational GenAI adoption stages.
topics: Information Systems Education and Curriculum Development

documents.abstract: As the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)–based educational technologies into teaching and learning processes accelerates, trust has emerged as a key determinant of whether preservice teachers are willing to adopt these technologies. The present study aimed to examine the relationship between the perceived trust of pre-service science teachers in AI-based educational technologies and generative AI acceptance and to determine the predictive power of trust on acceptance. Grounded in the TAM, the study employed a cross-sectional correlational survey design to investigate the role of trust in acceptance processes. Data were collected from 270 pre-service science teachers enrolled in a science teacher education program at a university via an online questionnaire. The Trust in AI-Based Educational Technologies Scale (TAI-EdTech Trust) and the Generative AI Acceptance Scale (GAIA) were used for data collection. The findings revealed a moderate, positive, and statistically significant relationship between trust in AI-based educational technologies and GA acceptance, indicating that trust significantly predicted GA acceptance. The results highlight the importance of developing content in science teacher education programs that supports the safe, ethical, and pedagogically responsible use of generative AI tools.

Large-language-model (LLM) layers are increasingly appended to electroencephalography (EEG) decoders, although their decision contribution is often unclear. We evaluate an uncertainty-driven architecture in which a calibrated EEG classifier predicts participants’ own four-level occupational-risk keypress ratings, a deterministic rule either retains or defers a prediction, and a template or optional LLM renders an auditable report. The objective is not to replace a previously published classifier benchmark on the shared EEG archive, but to evaluate downstream decisions from a fixed frozen-representation decoder. The analysis used 2634 response-inclusive 3 s epochs from 31 retained workers. Subject-grouped three-fold evaluation yielded balanced accuracy of 0.6336 (95% CI 0.5745–0.6622) and accuracy of 0.6875. Peak probability distinguished correct from incorrect predictions only moderately (AUC 0.6529), and the coverage-risk relationship was non-monotonic. At tau = 0.5, 71.49% of trials were retained (balanced accuracy of 0.6829); with illustrative under-estimation/over-estimation/deferral costs of 5/0.5/1, normalized cost fell from 0.5816 to 0.5363, but sensitivity analysis showed that benefit depends on the cost setting and threshold. A rule engine reproduced all evaluated LLM risk/deferral decisions, while a deterministic template matched the prespecified reporting checks; therefore, no decision-performance advantage of the LLM was demonstrated. The study supports cross-participant prediction within the shared experimental setting, not stimulus-disjoint generalization or objective workplace-risk prediction. Because response timestamps and actual supervisor decisions were unavailable, motor/visual confounding cannot be excluded and the human handoff remains a simulated policy rather than a human–AI team evaluation.

ABSTRACT As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technology rapidly permeates higher education, it creates opportunities to transform teaching, research, and workforce preparation while raising ethical, social and environmental concerns. Academic scientists have a unique role in this transition as their early exposure to publicly accessible GenAI tools shapes emerging practices, norms, and institutional responses. Existing research often treats AI‐related risk as a single construct, limiting understanding of how distinct risk dimensions shape regulatory preferences. This study investigates how academic scientists’ experience with GenAI relates to risk perceptions over agency loss and data breach, and how these perceptions are associated with their regulatory attitudes during its formative stage. Using survey data collected between September and November 2023, shortly after ChatGPT became widely accessible, we find that greater GenAI experience is associated with lower perceived risks. Meanwhile, different risk perceptions are linked to distinct regulatory preferences: perceived risk of agency loss is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation and a lower likelihood of supporting academic self‐regulation, whereas perceived data breach risk is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation but not associated with the likelihood of supporting self‐regulation. These findings provide an early baseline understanding of faculty attitudes toward GenAI regulation in academic contexts.

documents.abstract: Purpose To develop a social complexity-based understanding of how and where artificial intelligence (AI) and generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can enhance the effectiveness of performance measurement and management (PMM) mediated organisational change. Design/methodology/approach This article draws on a social complexity interpretation of PMM, conviction narrative theory and the AI and GAI literature, to present a conceptualisation of AI-augmented PMM-mediated organisational change that describes how and where machine-based and human-based decision-making processes can augment performance measurement systems and performance management practices. Findings AI's and GAI's inability to replicate human reflexivity and judgement in equivocal and indeterminate situations limits what these technologies can do in PMM-mediated organisational change. AI and GAI can augment decision-making processes associated with performance measurement and the execution of performance management-initiated interventions; however, creating these interventions relies on human reflexivity and judgement. Originality/value This conceptual investigation highlights the limitations of AI and GAI technologies in PMM-mediated organisational change and explains why human-based decision-making continues to play a distinctive role. It contributes to our understanding of how AI and GAI can influence organisational change in general, and performance management in particular, with implications for PMM researchers and practitioners.

Purpose This study aims to analyze the linear structural relationships and nonlinear predictive contributions associated with tourist satisfaction in the Trusmi Batik Tourism Area. By integrating PLS-SEM, ANN, and SHAP-based XAI, it evaluates how destination attributes function as hygiene or motivator factors. The ultimate goal is to develop a strategic quadrant matrix to guide local governments and destination managers in optimizing craft-based cultural tourism management. Design/methodology/approach This study employs a multi-stage hybrid design integrating PLS-SEM, an MLP-based artificial neural network (ANN) and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) using SHAP analysis. PLS-SEM evaluates linear structural relationships based on the proposed theoretical hypotheses. A parsimonious single-hidden-layer ANN captures complex, nonlinear predictive patterns. Finally, SHAP values interpret the model's hidden predictive contributions to construct an actionable strategic quadrant matrix. Findings The findings suggest that accessibility, resources, and the environment emerged as the primary “Star” motivators, with accessibility showing the strongest structural contribution and predictive importance among the examined constructs (ß = 0.310; |ϕ| = 0.416). “Batik Arts” emerged as the most influential indicator within the dataset. Services occupied the “Foundation” quadrant, whereas Facilities functioned primarily as a baseline hygiene factor and did not exhibit a statistically significant structural relationship with tourist satisfaction (ß = 0.014, p = 0.888). The parsimonious single-hidden-layer ANN demonstrated promising predictive performance in capturing nonlinear patterns within this exploratory dataset. Research limitations/implications This study integrates PLS-SEM, ANN, and SHAP-based XAI to examine linear and nonlinear patterns associated with tourist satisfaction within craft-based cultural tourism destinations. The findings suggest prioritizing immersive batik workshops, walkable heritage corridors, digital visitor information, and routine maintenance of basic facilities. The small, geographically focused sample limits generalizability and supports the need for external validation using larger and more diverse datasets. Practical implications This study offers a practical reference for tourism operators and local authorities to improve strategic resource allocation. Instead of funding costly luxury hotel expansions, managers could prioritize maintaining hygiene assets, including toilets, seating, and worship facilities. To enhance visitor satisfaction, investments may emphasize “Star” motivators through immersive batik-making workshops and authentic cultural experiences. Local governments may also improve urban micro-mobility by developing walkable sidewalks and flexible motorcycle routes throughout Trusmi's historic heritage corridors. These evidence-based recommendations support sustainable destination management while strengthening visitor experiences, cultural preservation, and long-term tourism resilience. Social implications This study has social implications for sustaining craft-based cultural tourism while strengthening community participation and cultural identity. The findings highlight the importance of accessible public spaces, immersive batik-making experiences, reliable visitor services, and heritage storytelling in supporting visitor engagement. Prioritizing these attributes can help local governments and tourism operators create more inclusive tourism environments that benefit visitors, artisans, and local communities. The framework also supports balanced resource allocation between basic hygiene facilities and culturally distinctive motivators. By strengthening artisan involvement, digital cultural communication, and heritage preservation, the approach can contribute to community resilience, intergenerational knowledge transmission, and sustainable tourism development. Originality/value The value of this study lies in its innovative hybrid framework integrating PLS-SEM, MLP-based ANN, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) within cultural tourism research. Compared with conventional linear approaches, the framework combines structural relationships, nonlinear predictive patterns, and SHAP-based interpretability to identify destination attributes with different levels of strategic importance.

The objective of the study is to investigate unethical issues in the use of Artificial intelligence (AI) among undergraduates in public Universities in Cross River State. The study was conducted in University of Calabar and University of Cross River State. Survey research design was adopted of the study. The population of this study comprised all final year students in the two public Universities in Cross River State. The population of final year students in University of Calabar and University of Cross River State comprised of 7,020 undergraduate students as recorded by Academic Planning Unit & Management Information System, 2023/2024 of the respective Universities. Stratified random sampling was adopted for the study. A total sample of 409 students which constitute 10% of the population of students in the study area sampling from population of 4081 students from fifty three (53) departments of University of Calabar and University of Cross River State. A questionnaire titled Unethical issues in the Use of Artificial intelligence Questionnaire (UIUAIQ) was developed by the researchers. This was subjected to face and content validity by three experts in measurement and evaluation in Faculty of Education University of Calabar. A trial tested on fifty (50) students from College of Health Technology Calabar to establish the reliability of the instrument. Cronbach Alpha coefficient was used to determine the reliability estimate of the instrument α = .70-.72. The instrument was administered to the respondents and retrieved with Zero attrition rate. This process was facilitated by the researcher and two trained research assistants. The data collected was analyzed through descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation. The findings of this study reveal a significant prevalence of unethical issues in the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) among undergraduates in public universities in Cross River State. Furthermore, the study also indicates a high level of overreliance on AI technologies among undergraduates, leading to reduced engagement in academic tasks and a decline in deep learning experiences. Based on the findings, it was recommended among others that Higher institutions should incorporate AI ethics education into their curriculum to sensitize students about the ethical implications of AI misuse.

documents.abstract: Generative AI has entered software work with remarkable speed, yet trust in its output remains unsettled. This study examines how developers and learners navigate AI-assisted software work through mental models and trust. Analyzing 40,052 responses from the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, the findings reveal a durable paradox: professionals use AI more intensively than learners but trust it less, evaluating its capability for complex tasks more cautiously. The primary threat to trust is corrective labor, such as debugging time, rather than code legibility. Cluster analysis identifies four mental-model profiles—open but light users, skeptical dependents, resistant/disengaged respondents, and enthusiastic adopters—with professionals disproportionately concentrated in skeptical dependence. Ultimately, adoption does not settle the trust question; instead, mental models act as interpretive filters through which developers decide when to rely, verify, and pull back.
